# Bulk import: throughput with an explicit recovery contract

[← All question groups](../index.md) · `sql-bulk-import` · **SQL Server & Data Engineering** · Catalog level: senior

<p>Questions come from the preserved source notes. Reframing, assessment intent, senior signals and rubrics are editorial interpretations, not verified model answers or universal interviewer expectations. Follow-ups and the combined production exercise are agent additions. Reading this bank creates no learning record, score, completion or review schedule.</p>

## Start with one representative question

[S03-Q027](#S03-Q027)

<p>How would you choose and validate an efficient way to insert 10,000 or more records into SQL Server?</p>

## One group objective and observable capabilities

<p>Design a resource-bounded import whose insertion and recovery behavior match the business contract.</p>

<ul>
<li>Compare row inserts, batching and bulk copy using equivalent input and transaction conditions.</li>
<li>Trace validation, buffering and database work to identify resource limits.</li>
<li>Choose all-or-nothing or partial-success semantics and explain safe retries.</li>
</ul>

**Prerequisites**

- [Concurrent transactions: protect an invariant and recover safely](sql-transactions-concurrency.md)

<p>How would you insert 10,000 or more records efficiently? First compare the data paths, then define what happens to valid and invalid rows. Buffering, transaction size and database maintenance interact; a faster happy path is insufficient when a late failure leaves an unclear result.</p>

### S03-Q028 · Mechanism

<p>Compare row-by-row inserts, batched inserts and bulk copy for a SQL Server import. What work and guarantees differ?</p>

**Source:** [S03-Q028](../../sources/03-sql-data-performance.md#q028)

<p class="scope-note">Version-sensitive scope: state the actual runtime/framework/provider and check official documentation before making technical claims. This question bank does not certify current behavior, product defaults or performance results.</p>

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S03-Q028](../../sources/03-sql-data-performance.md#q028)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> Compare row-by-row insert, batching and bulk copy approaches.

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>Trace how data reaches the database in each approach. Compare call overhead and processing boundaries alongside correctness requirements.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Compare insertion mechanisms using the same workload and contract.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>Name SQL Server and client-provider versions, batch sizes and transaction options. Verify bulk-copy behavior and options in official documentation rather than assuming identical guarantees.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Describes the data path and where each approach performs validation or database work.</li>
<li>Defines comparable tests and explains which constraint could favor a different approach.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Ranking approaches by speed without fixing transaction, validation and input conditions.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

### S03-Q027 · Application

<p>How would you choose and validate an efficient way to insert 10,000 or more records into SQL Server?</p>

**Source:** [S03-Q027](../../sources/03-sql-data-performance.md#q027)

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S03-Q027](../../sources/03-sql-data-performance.md#q027)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> How would you insert 10,000+ records efficiently?

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>Start from the import requirements, then propose a data path and a comparison. The row count alone is not enough to select an implementation.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Turn an import requirement into a measurable insertion strategy.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>State row sizes, validation rules, acceptable failure behavior, network path and concurrent workload. Treat the scenario as hypothetical until tests are supplied.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Explains the proposed data flow and the bottleneck it is intended to address.</li>
<li>Checks correctness, elapsed time and resource costs under equivalent inputs.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Naming bulk copy as the answer without considering validation, transactions or workload constraints.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>How would you compare candidates if production traffic must remain responsive during the import?</li>
</ul>

<a id="S03-Q030"></a>

### S03-Q030 · Application

<p>How would you validate and import a large dataset while keeping memory usage bounded?</p>

**Source:** [S03-Q030](../../sources/03-sql-data-performance.md#q030)

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S03-Q030](../../sources/03-sql-data-performance.md#q030)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> How would you validate and import a large dataset without excessive memory usage?

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>Design the path from input reading through validation to persistence. Explain where data waits and how much must be retained at once.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Design an import pipeline whose memory needs do not grow unchecked with the file.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>State input format, validation rules, dependency latency and the allowed treatment of invalid rows. Include cancellation and failure reporting; no file or benchmark is provided.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Explains bounded buffers and how a slow database affects input processing.</li>
<li>Identifies validation that needs cross-row context and a way to check resource limits.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Reading the entire file into memory or creating unbounded parallel tasks while calling the pipeline streaming.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>How would you handle a rule that detects duplicates across the whole file?</li>
</ul>

</details>

<a id="S03-Q031"></a>

### S03-Q031 · Failure cases

<p>If an import fails near the end, when would you roll back the whole import, and when would you retain valid rows and report failures?</p>

**Source:** [S03-Q031](../../sources/03-sql-data-performance.md#q031)

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S03-Q031](../../sources/03-sql-data-performance.md#q031)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> If processing fails late in the import, when should you rollback everything versus retain valid rows and report failures?

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>Define the business meaning of success before choosing recovery behavior. Explain what the user can safely do after receiving a partial result.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Choose an import failure contract and defend its recovery implications.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>State whether rows are independent, which failures occurred and the retry/resume requirements. Do not silently change an all-or-nothing requirement into partial success.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Connects the choice to business consistency and a clear per-job/per-row outcome.</li>
<li>Handles retry, reconciliation and error reporting without losing or duplicating accepted work.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Choosing the faster approach without defining the resulting data state or user contract.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>How would a retry know which rows have already been accepted?</li>
</ul>

</details>

### S03-Q029 · Trade-offs

<p>How do transaction size, logging, indexes and constraints influence a bulk-write workload? How would you distinguish their effects?</p>

**Source:** [S03-Q029](../../sources/03-sql-data-performance.md#q029)

<p class="scope-note">Version-sensitive scope: state the actual runtime/framework/provider and check official documentation before making technical claims. This question bank does not certify current behavior, product defaults or performance results.</p>

<details markdown="1" class="question-original">
<summary>Original source wording and provenance</summary>

**[S03-Q029](../../sources/03-sql-data-performance.md#q029)**

<div lang="en" markdown="1">

> How do transaction size, logging, indexes and constraints affect bulk-write performance?

</div>

</details>

<details markdown="1" class="question-guidance">
<summary>What the question asks and how to assess an attempt</summary>

**What to clarify**

<p>Relate each factor to database work and recovery requirements. Propose measurements that separate competing explanations for slow imports.</p>

**Inferred assessment intent**

<p>Explain bulk-write costs and test a targeted change.</p>

**Scope and important assumptions**

<p>Specify SQL Server version, recovery model, table/index state and chosen import options. Check official logging and constraint behavior before relying on configuration-specific claims.</p>

**Observable signs of a strong senior answer**

<ul>
<li>Connects the factors to throughput, contention, resource usage and correctness requirements.</li>
<li>Changes one relevant factor at a time and verifies recovery as well as speed.</li>
</ul>

**Misconceptions and shallow answers to watch for**

<ul>
<li>Disabling safeguards or changing logging assumptions solely to maximize one throughput number.</li>
</ul>

**Related follow-ups — agent-added**

<ul>
<li>What would you inspect if larger batches stop improving throughput but increase recovery time?</li>
</ul>

</details>

## Combined production exercise — agent-added

<p>Design a .NET worker importing a large CSV into SQL Server while normal API traffic continues. Memory is limited and malformed rows may appear near the end. Declare whether the job is atomic or allows partial success, choose an insertion approach, then define cancellation, retry/resume, result reporting and the measurements needed to compare it with a baseline.</p>

## Short rubric — use only with an actual attempt

**Basic answer**

<p>Names a viable insertion approach and a clear treatment of invalid rows.</p>

**Senior answer**

<p>Traces bounded data flow, validates provider options, and defends failure/retry semantics alongside workload-level resource and throughput checks.</p>

**Still needs evidence**

<p>No pipeline/design artifact, failure-state examples or comparable measurements are supplied; efficiency and safe recovery remain proposals.</p>
